exercises.title: A RUN WITHOUT A WINNER
exercises.context:
Match seven paragraphs to seven of the eight headings. Use each selected heading once; one is extra.
A. Returning becomes its own achievement
B. How professional runners choose sponsors
C. A different invitation
D. The format does not suit everyone
E. Choosing a personal pace
F. A conversation changes the experience
G. Work behind the visible activity
H. Numbers used for a limited purpose
1. The notice for the Saturday run promised neither prizes nor a finishing order. Participants could run, jog or walk the
same short route. For Daniel, who had avoided organised sport since school, that wording mattered more than the
distance. It suggested that arriving last would not mean failing.
2. At the start, a volunteer explained that faster participants should leave space for others. Daniel initially tried to keep up
with someone ahead, then slowed down enough to speak comfortably. Nobody told him that this was a disappointing
choice. The activity allowed him to adjust his effort rather than follow somebody else's target.
3. Before anyone arrived, volunteers had checked the path and placed signs at two turns. Others remained at the finish to
welcome participants and collect equipment. Running was only one way to contribute. A person who could not join the
route could still be essential to making the morning work.
4. The organisers counted participants to understand how much space and support the event needed. They did not publish
a ranked list. This distinction helped Daniel accept being counted: the number served an operational purpose without
turning his morning into a public comparison with people who had different experience and goals.
5. Halfway round, Daniel began talking to another walker about a building beside the path. The conversation made him
notice his surroundings instead of repeatedly checking how far remained. He had expected exercise to be the main reason
to return. The chance of an undemanding conversation became equally important.
6. Some experienced runners preferred events with recorded times and competitive targets. The organisers did not claim
their approach was better for every person. They were offering a different kind of occasion. A clear description helped

people choose whether it matched what they wanted, without presenting competition itself as a problem.
7. Daniel came back the following week and recognised several faces. He had not suddenly become an enthusiastic
athlete, and he did not plan to enter a race. The meaningful change was smaller: he had found an activity he was willing to
repeat. For him, consistency mattered more than a dramatic first performance.

exercises.title: A SUITCASE WITH NO WHEELS
exercises.context:
Match seven paragraphs to seven of the eight headings. Use each selected heading once; one is extra.

A. The limits of the available record
B. An argument for travelling without luggage
C. A different way of looking
D. A trade brought back to life
E. Evidence that contradicts a guess
F. A repair designed to remain visible
G. A useful object becomes a puzzle
H. Following a geographical clue
1. At a second-hand shop, Lena found a small leather suitcase with a broken handle. Inside was a railway label bearing a
town name she did not recognise. She bought the case to store drawings, but the label made her curious about its
previous owner.
2. An online map produced no result for the name. An older atlas in the library did: the town had been renamed after two
neighbouring districts joined. Knowing its present name allowed Lena to locate a local archive and send a photograph of
the label.
3. Lena had assumed the case belonged to a wealthy holidaymaker. The archivist disagreed. Its unusual internal straps
resembled those used to secure samples carried by travelling salespeople. A faded company stamp beneath the lining
supported that explanation more convincingly than the attractive leather did.
4. The company had supplied buttons to clothing shops. Its representatives travelled with tiny examples of each design,
arranged so buyers could compare colours quickly. The suitcase was therefore a portable showroom. Scratches inside it
probably came from the metal sample boards rather than from ordinary packing.
5. No surviving document identified the person who had carried this particular case. Lena resisted adding an imaginary
owner to make the story more exciting. She could explain its likely function and period of use, but a complete personal
history remained beyond what the evidence justified.
6. For the handle, a craftsperson suggested new leather in a slightly different shade. Matching the original perfectly would
have hidden the repair. Lena preferred the contrast: anyone examining the case could distinguish its old parts from the
work needed to make it usable again.
7. The case now holds Lena's drawings, as originally planned. Yet she pays more attention to ordinary objects around her.
A mark beneath a chair or a handwritten note inside a book may explain how something was used, even when it reveals
nothing about its monetary value.

exercises.title: WHAT HAPPENS TO AN UNDELIVERABLE PARCEL?
exercises.context:
Match seven paragraphs to seven of the eight headings. Use each selected heading once; one is extra.

A. A small improvement before dispatch
B. A correction needs to reach the right system
C. The journey can run backwards
D. Storage has an operational purpose
E. Why customers should collect every delivery
F. Two sources of information are compared
G. Why the contents are not the first clue
H. An address that passes the first check
1. A parcel can enter a delivery network even when its address is incomplete. The postcode may identify a real street,
while the building number is missing. Automated systems accept the broad destination; the difficulty becomes apparent
only when a driver needs to find one particular door.
2. At the depot, staff compare the printed label with the electronic booking. Sometimes one contains a detail absent from
the other. A flat number entered online may have been cut off when the sender printed the label. Restoring it solves the
problem without opening the package.
3. Opening a parcel immediately would create privacy and handling problems. Staff first use the contact details supplied for
the sender or recipient. Any later inspection follows the carrier's procedures. The fact that a package is difficult to deliver
does not make its contents freely available for investigation.
4. Phoning the driver is not always enough. A corrected address must usually be attached to the parcel's record, otherwise
the next shift may see the same incomplete label. A temporary conversation can solve today's question while leaving
tomorrow's worker with precisely the original problem.
5. Undeliverable parcels are kept apart from items ready for dispatch. This reduces the chance of repeatedly sending an
unresolved package along the same route. The separate area is therefore part of the tracking process, although its shelves
may look like a collection of unrelated mistakes.
6. When contact attempts fail, the parcel may return to the sender, subject to the service's rules. That journey still requires
a usable address. Senders who omit their own details remove an important recovery route, even if they correctly assume
that recipients are the main destination.
7. The most effective check is often unglamorous: read the printed label after producing it. Check that the name, building
number and postcode remain visible and that an old label has been removed. A correct online form cannot compensate for
an unreadable or contradictory physical label.

exercises.title: THE PLEASURE OF BEING A BEGINNER
exercises.context:
Match seven paragraphs to seven of the eight headings. Use each selected heading once; one is extra.

A. Failure provides more precise information
B. Comparison depends on what is visible
C. Why talent should decide who attends
D. A lesson beyond the workshop
E. Practice needs a manageable target
F. A demonstration does not equal understanding
G. Competence can become a hiding place
H. An imperfect result can remain valuable
1. I had spent years choosing leisure activities I was already good at. Then a friend persuaded me to join a pottery class.
My first bowl collapsed before I could lift it from the wheel. The embarrassment revealed how carefully I had been
protecting my reputation as a capable person.
2. Watching the tutor shape clay looked reassuringly simple. Trying it exposed what the demonstration concealed:
pressure had to change continuously as the material moved. I could repeat the instructions aloud without being able to
perform them. Knowledge of the steps was only the beginning of learning.
3. The tutor did not call my second attempt bad. She showed where one wall had become thinner than the other and asked
me to notice the pressure of my left hand. A visible fault gave us a specific question to investigate, which was more useful
than a general judgement about ability.
4. Across the room, another beginner produced a remarkably even cup. Later I discovered that he repaired musical
instruments for a living. His experience with delicate manual work was relevant, despite his lack of pottery lessons. The
label 'beginner' had concealed an important difference between us.
5. For several sessions I concentrated on making walls of equal thickness. Decoration could wait. Limiting my attention did
not make the activity less creative; it gave me enough control to attempt new shapes later. Trying to improve everything at
once had previously left me unsure what caused each result.
6. I still use one early cup, although its handle is awkward. It reminds me of the decisions I made and the problems I
eventually understood. Keeping it is not a claim that quality is irrelevant. It is a way of recognising progress that a flawless
purchased object could never record.
7. Now, when I avoid something because I might look foolish, I ask whether competence is actually required before
starting. Some activities involve serious risks and demand proper instruction. Many others simply require accepting a
period of visible uncertainty. That period can be enjoyable once it stops feeling like a verdict.

exercises.title: WHY A CLEAR APOLOGY IS DIFFICULT TO WRITE
exercises.context:
Match seven paragraphs to seven of the eight headings. Use each selected heading once; one is extra.
A. A promise needs a practical boundary
B. Not every reader needs every detail
C. The advantages of saying nothing
D. The final test is the reader's next step
E. Naming the event reduces uncertainty
F. Reasons can be mistaken for excuses
G. Warmth comes from attention
H. A message that evades its own purpose
1. The theatre's email began, 'We regret any inconvenience that may have been experienced.' Its audience already knew
the cancelled performance had caused inconvenience. The uncertain phrasing made a definite event sound hypothetical.
Readers had to work out both what the theatre acknowledged and whether it accepted any responsibility.
2. A clearer opening would identify the cancellation and its effect: 'We are sorry that Friday's performance was cancelled
after you arrived.' This statement does not explain everything, but it establishes shared facts. Readers can then judge the
explanation that follows without first decoding an abstract reference to inconvenience.
3. An explanation about a technical fault may be necessary, particularly if customers wonder whether the next performance
is safe. Placing it before the apology, however, can suggest that the organisation is defending itself. The same information
can produce a different impression when its position in the message changes.
4. 'We will make this right' sounds reassuring but tells a customer little. Stating when a refund will arrive is more useful. If
the date is uncertain, the message should explain when an update will be sent. Precision is possible even when the final
outcome is not yet known.
5. The engineer's full account belongs in an internal report. A customer mainly needs to know what happened, what action
is required and what the theatre will do next. Removing technical detail is appropriate when it improves relevance;
concealing a material fact would be a very different editorial choice.
6. Some writers try to make an apology friendly by adding cheerful punctuation. A more convincing approach is to
recognise a specific consequence, such as a wasted journey. That observation shows the reader's situation has been
considered. Tone depends on the substance of the message as much as on its vocabulary.
7. Before sending the revised email, the writer should ask what a customer can now do. If a refund requires a form, include
the route to it. If no action is needed, say so. An apology becomes effective communication when it reduces the uncertainty
created by the original failure.

exercises.title: A STATION CLOCK AND A MISSED CONNECTION
exercises.context:
Match seven paragraphs to seven of the eight headings. Use each selected heading once; one is extra.

A. A deliberately less complete display
B. The apparently obvious explanation
C. A proposal to remove all timetables
D. The investigation changes its question
E. Testing under an unusual condition
F. Trust includes the admission of uncertainty
G. Two displays represent different moments
H. An unnoticed cue loses its meaning
1. When a passenger missed her connection, she blamed the station clock. It showed 10:12 as her train departed,
although the timetable listed 10:14. The station team initially treated the complaint as a faulty-clock report. A recording
from the platform camera complicated that explanation: the train had left at the correct time.
2. The large clock was accurate. The passenger had photographed an information screen displaying the time at which its
connection to the network had stopped. Unlike the clock, this smaller display had frozen. Its familiar appearance made it
seem current even after the information had ceased to update.
3. A tiny warning symbol had appeared in one corner of the screen. Staff who maintained the system recognised it
immediately; passengers did not. The symbol had been designed to identify a technical condition, not to explain what that
condition meant for someone deciding whether there was time to buy coffee.
4. Engineers could repair the network fault, but the design team asked a broader question: how should a screen behave
when it can no longer confirm its information? Preserving the last display looked tidy. Replacing it with an explicit warning
would be less elegant but would stop outdated data looking authoritative.
5. The revised design removed departure estimates when the connection failed and directed passengers to the staffed
desk. This reduced the quantity of information on screen. It increased its honesty. The designers accepted that a visible
gap was preferable to a confident answer that the system could no longer support.
6. The team simulated a connection failure during a quiet period and observed whether passengers noticed the warning.
Testing only normal operation would have missed the original problem. The useful question was not whether people liked
the screen, but whether their behaviour changed when its information became unreliable.
7. The incident shows why a service should reveal the limits of what it knows. A blank estimate can be frustrating, yet it
allows a traveller to seek another source. An apparently precise estimate removes that incentive. Accuracy therefore
depends partly on communicating when accuracy cannot be guaranteed.

exercises.title: WHEN A TRANSLATION BECOMES A LOCAL PRODUCT
exercises.context:
Match seven paragraphs to seven of the eight headings. Use each selected heading once; one is extra.
A. Space imposes a hidden constraint
B. A joke is replaced to preserve its effect
C. Consistency is not identical wording
D. Changes must travel back to the source
E. Review without context has limits
F. Words are only one layer
G. Quality is judged through use
H. The disappearance of all regional differences
1. A game translated into another language may still feel unfamiliar. Its jokes, instructions and assumptions about
politeness can depend on the culture in which it was written. Localisation teams therefore examine what a player is
expected to understand, rather than treating every sentence as an isolated piece of vocabulary.
2. A button that comfortably holds a short English verb may be too narrow for its translated equivalent. Shrinking the font
can make the interface unreadable. Translators and designers may need to choose a different phrase or resize the
element, so a linguistic decision becomes a layout decision as well.
3. One puzzle relied on two English words sounding alike. A literal translation would preserve the words while destroying
the clue. The local team wrote a different sound-based joke that led to the same solution. In this case, changing the
surface wording was necessary to retain the player's experience.
4. Characters may address a player differently depending on their relationship. Forcing every speaker to use the same
polite form can flatten those distinctions. A terminology guide needs to separate technical consistency from character
voice; otherwise a tool intended to prevent confusion may make the dialogue less believable.
5. A reviewer reading a spreadsheet may approve a sentence that sounds wrong when spoken during a fast-moving
scene. The line might be too long, or it may reveal information before the player sees the relevant object. Testing the
translated version inside the game exposes problems that language review alone cannot.

6. When a developer alters an instruction, every affected language version needs the update. If teams exchange separate
files without tracking changes, an old warning may survive in one version. A shared record of decisions protects accuracy
more effectively than relying on each translator's memory of previous discussions.
7. Players rarely praise an instruction for having been translated correctly. They simply follow it. Successful localisation
often goes unnoticed because nothing interrupts the activity. That invisibility should not be confused with a lack of creative
work: it may be the result of many small, carefully coordinated departures from literal wording.

exercises.title: SHOULD EVERY PHOTOGRAPH BE KEPT?
exercises.context:
Match seven paragraphs to seven of the eight headings. Use each selected heading once; one is extra.
A. An imperfect compromise between extremes
B. Quantity can obstruct retrieval
C. Storage changes the decision
D. Ownership creates another responsibility
E. Descriptions restore missing context
F. How to choose a more expensive camera
G. Selection is a form of authorship
H. The best picture is not always the best record
1. When each exposure used a frame of film, taking a photograph involved a small commitment. Digital storage made that
commitment almost disappear. The difficult decision moved from before the picture to after it: which of hundreds of similar
images deserves attention, and who will ever make that choice?
2. Keeping everything seems safer than deleting something valuable. Yet a collection becomes less useful when finding
one image requires scrolling through dozens of near-identical versions. The cost is paid in attention rather than storage
space. A technically complete archive may therefore become practically inaccessible to its owner.
3. A blurred photograph may show the only image of a room before it was demolished. A sharp, attractive one may reveal
less. Choosing solely on visual quality can remove evidence that later acquires personal or historical value. Selection
depends on the purpose of the collection, which may itself change over time.
4. One approach is to keep a small, clearly organised selection for everyday use while storing the remaining files
separately. This avoids forcing immediate deletion decisions. It also acknowledges that the accessible collection and the
complete archive serve different purposes, rather than expecting one folder to perform both tasks equally well.
5. A date supplied automatically by a camera cannot identify who appears in the picture or why the event mattered. Brief
captions written while memories are fresh can add more value than keeping ten additional shots. Without that information,
future viewers may have evidence of an occasion but no way to interpret it.

6. Photographs often show people other than the person maintaining the collection. A picture suitable for private storage
may be inappropriate for public sharing. Decisions about preservation and publication should therefore remain separate.
The wish to organise an archive does not remove the need to consider the expectations of those depicted.
7. An album tells a story through what it includes and omits. Recognising that does not make selection dishonest; it makes
the choices visible. A useful archive allows viewers to understand how it was assembled. The aim is not perfect neutrality,
but enough context to prevent a selective collection appearing complete.

exercises.title: THE QUEUE NOBODY COULD SEE
exercises.context:
Match seven paragraphs to seven of the eight headings. Use each selected heading once; one is extra.
A. A number can imply more certainty than exists
B. A fair-looking system creates resentment
C. The measure chosen shapes the service
D. Efficiency and fairness answer different questions
E. Too much detail creates a new burden
F. Individual exceptions still require human judgement
G. An explanation can change an interpretation
H. Why all appointments should be abolished
1. A service centre replaced its physical queue with appointment numbers sent to visitors' phones. The waiting room
became quieter, yet complaints increased. People who arrived later sometimes entered first. The system was applying
different appointment categories correctly, but visitors could no longer see any intelligible relationship between waiting and
being served.
2. Managers measured the average time needed to complete each case. Visitors judged whether their own wait made
sense. A specialist dealing quickly with simple cases could improve the average while making a person with a complex
case feel repeatedly overlooked. Neither observation necessarily disproved the other; they described different experiences
of the same process.
3. Staff began telling visitors that separate teams handled different requests. A later arrival might therefore join another
queue rather than move ahead in the same one. This explanation did not shorten anyone's wait. It removed an incorrect
inference that had made the delay seem personally unfair.
4. Publishing the full scheduling rules proved unhelpful. Visitors had to interpret exceptions and specialist categories while
already anxious about their own cases. A simpler message explained the principle and gave an estimated range.
Transparency worked best when it answered the question people actually had, rather than exposing every internal
procedure.

5. The centre initially displayed an exact predicted call time. Complex cases made that prediction unstable, and each
revision looked like a broken promise. Replacing it with a range was less precise but more realistic. Staff also explained
what would happen if a visitor had still not been called by its upper limit.
6. No scheduling rule could anticipate every need. A visitor who required language support or had difficulty remaining
seated might need assistance without being moved automatically to the front. Staff needed authority to respond to the
particular problem. Otherwise the apparently impartial system could produce avoidable hardship through rigid consistency.
7. The centre retained its digital queue but added questions about whether visitors understood their wait. The change
recognised a limitation in the original target. Speed remained valuable, yet a fast service that people experienced as
arbitrary was not fully successful. Evaluation improved once the organisation measured the quality of the experience as
well as its duration.

exercises.title: THE LONG JOURNEY OF THE WEATHER FORECAST
exercises.context:
Match seven paragraphs to seven of the eight headings. Use each selected heading once; one is extra.
A. Several outcomes can be more informative than one
B. Improvement depends on looking backwards
C. Observations before instruments
D. Calculation turns patterns into projections
E. Why one forecasting method must replace all others
F. Users need consequences as well as numbers
G. Communication makes a wider picture possible
H. Standardisation improves the raw material
1. People have always watched the sky for signs of approaching weather. Farmers, sailors and travellers built up detailed
knowledge of local patterns long before forecasts became a public service. Such knowledge could be remarkably useful
within a familiar landscape, but it was difficult to transfer. A cloud formation that preceded rain near one mountain range
might mean something different elsewhere. Nor could an observer on the coast know that a storm was developing far
beyond the horizon. The central limitation was therefore not simply a lack of careful observation. It was the inability to
compare observations from distant places quickly enough for them to describe the same developing situation.
2. The spread of rapid long-distance communication changed what forecasters could attempt. Reports collected at roughly
the same time could be placed on a map, revealing patterns that no single observer could see. The weather was no longer
merely a sequence of local surprises; it became a moving system that could be followed across a region. This did not
instantly make predictions reliable. Stations used different instruments and reporting practices, and gaps remained
between them. Nevertheless, assembling simultaneous information created the basis for a new kind of inference. A
disturbance observed to the west could become a warning for places that had not yet experienced any change.
3. Before observations could be combined confidently, people had to agree on how to make them. Temperature readings
taken in direct sunlight cannot be compared fairly with readings from a shaded enclosure. The height and position of
instruments matter, as does the time at which a measurement is recorded. Standard procedures made differences
between stations more meaningful by reducing differences caused by the act of measuring. This work lacked the drama of
predicting a major storm, but it was essential. A sophisticated calculation cannot recover the true state of the atmosphere
from inconsistent data merely because the calculation itself is precise.
4. Mathematical models introduced another change. Instead of relying entirely on resemblance to previous weather
situations, forecasters could estimate how the present atmosphere would evolve according to physical relationships.
Computers made increasingly detailed calculations practical. Yet a model remained a representation, with the world
divided into manageable sections and some processes simplified. Making those sections smaller required more computing
power and better observations. Improvements were therefore gradual rather than magical. A colourful map produced by a
computer might appear more authoritative than an older hand-drawn chart, but both depended on assumptions and on the

quality of the information available when they were made.
5. Small differences in the estimated starting conditions can lead to different later outcomes. One way to explore that
uncertainty is to run multiple related forecasts rather than treating a single result as inevitable. If the runs broadly agree,
confidence may be higher; if they diverge, the range itself becomes useful information. This approach can frustrate people
who expect one definite answer. However, a probability is not necessarily an admission that forecasting has failed. It can
be a more honest description of the evidence than a simple claim that rain will, or will not, occur at a particular location
tomorrow afternoon.
6. A forecast acquires practical value when someone can use it to decide what to do. The same likelihood of heavy rain
may matter differently to a commuter, an outdoor-event organiser and a farmer harvesting a crop. Communicating only the
meteorological information leaves each user to translate it into possible consequences. Clear warnings help by explaining
the relevant impact without pretending that every situation is identical. They also need to distinguish confidence from
severity: an event can be unlikely but serious enough to justify preparation. Choosing understandable language is
therefore part of forecasting, rather than a decorative stage added after the scientific work has finished.
7. Forecasting organisations compare predictions with what subsequently happened. This examination can reveal a
persistent regional bias or a tendency to underestimate certain conditions. It is not enough to remember the spectacular
successes and failures, because memorable events form an unrepresentative sample. Systematic records show whether a
change actually improves performance across many cases. The modern forecast is consequently both a statement about
the future and the product of repeated evaluation of the past. Its history is not a straight journey from ignorance to
certainty, but a continuing effort to measure more consistently, calculate more usefully and describe the remaining
uncertainty more clearly.

exercises.title: THE ROOM THAT TEACHES YOU TO LISTEN
exercises.context:
Match seven paragraphs to seven of the eight headings. Use each selected heading once; one is extra.
A. Materials change what remains audible
B. Flexibility comes with a practical cost
C. Reflections arrive after the original sound
D. A surprising first impression
E. Good design supports the intended activity
F. A campaign to close large concert venues
G. The audience is part of the room
H. A familiar seat can conceal a local problem
1. On entering a small rehearsal room, a visiting pianist played a familiar sequence and stopped almost immediately. The
notes seemed unusually dry. In the concert hall next door, the same passage had sounded rich and continuous. Nothing
had changed in the piano or the player's technique; the room was altering what reached the listener. This everyday
experience introduces a difficult design problem. A space suitable for clear speech may not provide the atmosphere
musicians want, while a room that flatters a solo instrument may turn a busy conversation into a confusing wash of sound.
There is no single acoustic quality that every activity requires.
2. Sound reaches an audience by more than one route. Some travels directly from its source, while some encounters
walls, ceilings or other surfaces first. These reflected sounds arrive later. Depending on their timing and strength, they can
enrich the impression of a performance or interfere with its clarity. A listener does not usually identify each reflection
separately. Instead, the combined result may feel warm, distant, harsh or muddled. Describing those impressions is easier
than connecting them to a particular feature of the room. The designer must work between subjective experience and
measurable behaviour, without assuming that either one can replace the other.
3. Soft furnishings tend to absorb more sound than hard, smooth surfaces, but simply adding as much absorption as
possible is not a universal solution. A room can become so acoustically dry that performers struggle to hear how their
sound develops. Different materials also affect different parts of the sound spectrum, so a treatment that reduces one
problem may leave another untouched. This is why a few attractive panels cannot be assumed to solve every acoustic
difficulty. Their position, depth and relationship to the rest of the room matter. Choosing them only for their appearance
treats a functional intervention as though it were ordinary decoration.
4. An empty hall may behave differently from the same hall during a performance. Clothing and bodies absorb sound, and
the distribution of people changes the environment the designer is trying to control. Testing only before an audience
arrives can therefore give an incomplete impression. Rehearsals and opening events often reveal adjustments that need to
be made. This does not necessarily show that the original calculations were careless. It shows that a building is used by
people rather than existing as a fixed, empty shape. The interaction between the intended activity and the occupied space
is part of the design problem itself.

5. Some venues use movable curtains, adjustable panels or other features to suit different events. In principle, this allows
one room to support both spoken presentations and musical performances. In practice, someone must know which
arrangement to select and have time to make the change. A flexible system that is difficult to operate may remain in the
same position for every booking. Its theoretical range then offers little benefit. The choice between a specialised room and
an adaptable one should therefore include staffing and everyday routines, rather than comparing only the possibilities
shown on an architect's drawing or in a supplier's demonstration.
6. Acoustic quality is not necessarily identical throughout a hall. A seat beneath a balcony may receive a different balance
of direct and reflected sound from one near the centre. People who always sit in the same place can form quite different
opinions of the same venue without either being mistaken. During evaluation, listening from several positions is more
informative than relying on one favourable location. It can also explain why a performer feels that a room sounds excellent
while some audience members disagree. The stage and the back row are different listening environments, even though
they belong to one building.
7. The rehearsal room that initially disappointed the pianist had a useful purpose. Its limited reverberation made uneven
playing easier to notice, so it supported precise practice. The concert hall served another purpose by allowing musical
phrases to blend more generously. Judging one as simply better would miss the distinction. A successful acoustic design
begins by asking what people need to hear and do in the space. Technical measurements help answer that question, but
they cannot choose the purpose on the users' behalf. The best room is not the one with the most impressive description; it
is the one that supports the work or experience for which it is used.

exercises.title: A TOWN CHOOSES WHAT TO PUT ON ITS EMPTY SHOPFRONTS
exercises.context:
Match seven paragraphs to seven of the eight headings. Use each selected heading once; one is extra.
A. One proposal offers a quick visual solution
B. A second option invites local authorship
C. An unexpected result shifts the emphasis
D. Why every empty shop should become a museum
E. A temporary project needs an ending
F. Commercial use creates competing incentives
G. A limited trial separates prediction from observation
H. The problem extends beyond appearance
1. The town's vacant shops had become a familiar subject in local conversation. Some residents complained about their
appearance, while traders worried that stretches of dark windows discouraged people from walking further along the street.
The council had little control over the speed at which private properties would be let. It could, however, negotiate
temporary use of their windows. The proposal sounded modest, but it raised a question about what the town wanted those
windows to communicate. Covering the glass would conceal vacancy; using it as a public surface could acknowledge the
problem while giving people a reason to pause and look.
2. The first option was to place large photographs of imaginary shop interiors behind the glass. Supporters argued that the
street would immediately appear more active. The images could be produced consistently and installed without requiring
much access to the buildings. Critics objected that a picture of a busy cafe might look convincing from a distance but
disappointing close up. There was also a risk that visitors would mistake an image for an actual business. The
disagreement concerned more than artistic taste. It asked whether improving the appearance of activity was an
appropriate response to the absence of activity itself.
3. Another proposal would allow schools, clubs and individual residents to display work. This offered variety and could
make the windows feel connected to the people who used the street. However, an invitation to participate would not
guarantee a balanced result. Groups with confident organisers might occupy most of the available space, while less
established voices remained absent. The council would need a selection process that was understandable without turning
a temporary display into a complicated competition. It would also have to decide who maintained the work, how long each
contribution stayed and what happened if a property became available to a tenant suddenly.
4. A third suggestion was to rent the windows for advertisements and use the income to maintain the street. This had an
obvious financial advantage. It also introduced a tension: the most profitable advertisers might have little connection with
the town, and a sequence of large advertisements could make the area feel less distinctive. Local traders asked whether
they would receive favourable rates, but that would reduce the money raised. The option therefore could not be judged
solely by its expected income. The council had to consider what kind of public environment the arrangement would
produce and whose interests the available space should serve.

5. Rather than committing every window to one approach, the council obtained permission to test different treatments on a
short section of the street. It recorded where people stopped and asked nearby traders whether visitors seemed confused
about which premises were open. The trial did not prove that a display could restore the local economy, and the organisers
avoided making that claim. Its narrower purpose was to identify obvious problems before extending the scheme. Observing
how people actually responded was more useful than counting expressions of support at a meeting, where participants
had been reacting to descriptions rather than completed installations.
6. The most frequently discussed display contained a sequence of photographs showing the same corner at different
dates. People pointed out changes and shared memories with companions. Unlike the imaginary interiors, it did not
suggest that a closed business was operating. Unlike a conventional advertisement, it rewarded close attention without
asking viewers to buy anything. Its popularity did not mean every window should become a historical display. It suggested
that the strongest installations gave people something to do mentally or socially. That finding helped the organisers refine
their selection criteria around engagement rather than around one particular visual style.
7. The final scheme used changing local displays under short agreements that allowed owners to reclaim windows when
tenants arrived. Each installation included a contact and removal date, so abandoned work would not become another sign
of neglect. The council also published the limited purpose of the project: to improve the experience of walking along the
street while longer-term economic changes took place. This distinction mattered. A temporary cultural use could make
vacancy less discouraging, but it could not substitute for viable businesses, accessible premises or realistic rents.
Recognising that boundary made the project more credible, not less worthwhile.

exercises.title: WHEN A USEFUL MEASURE BECOMES A MISLEADING TARGET
exercises.context:
Match seven paragraphs to seven of the eight headings. Use each selected heading once; one is extra.
A. Visible improvement can conceal unfinished work
B. A target should remain open to revision
C. Why organisations should stop collecting information
D. The easiest cases become unusually attractive
E. Adding measures does not remove the need for judgement
F. Sampling restores some of the missing context
G. An indicator acquires a second job
H. Comparisons depend on the cases included
1. A support team began recording how quickly it answered customer messages. At first, the figure helped managers
identify busy periods and arrange staffing. Later, it became the principal target used to judge individual performance. The
number itself had not changed, but its role had. What had been a description of activity now influenced how people
behaved. Staff had a reason to reduce the measured interval even when doing so did not improve the customer's
experience. This transition is easy to overlook because a familiar measure appears to retain its familiar meaning. In
practice, the incentives attached to it can change the process it was intended to describe.
2. The team soon answered messages more rapidly. Some replies, however, merely confirmed that a request had been
received and promised a fuller response later. Customers still waited for their problems to be resolved, sometimes through
several exchanges. A chart of first-response times suggested improvement while saying little about completion. The initial
reply was not useless: acknowledgement can reassure a customer. The error lay in treating one stage of the service as
though it represented the whole. A measure can be accurate about what it counts and still support a misleading conclusion
when readers assume that it captures more than it actually does.
3. Once speed affected individual evaluations, straightforward requests became more desirable than complicated ones. An
employee could clear several simple questions in the time required to investigate a single difficult case. No explicit
instruction told staff to avoid complexity, yet the target made that behaviour rational. Customers with unusual problems
consequently risked receiving a slower service. This pattern did not require dishonesty or indifference. It arose from a
mismatch between the organisation's broad purpose and the narrower activity it rewarded. Explaining the gap as a failure
of employee motivation would therefore leave the underlying incentive unchanged and make the same outcome likely to
recur.
4. Managers responded by tracking resolution time and customer satisfaction as well. The additional information was
useful, but it introduced further questions. Some requests depended on outside suppliers, making rapid resolution
impossible. Some customers were dissatisfied because the correct answer was not the answer they wanted. Combining
several numbers into one score could conceal these distinctions rather than resolve them. A broader set of measures
should support informed discussion about performance, not create the impression that every relevant consideration has

been captured mathematically. The task is to understand why the figures differ, including whether those differences are
within the team's control.
5. One branch appeared consistently slower than another until managers examined the requests each handled. The
slower branch received a larger share of complex account problems. Comparing their averages without acknowledging
that difference made a demanding workload look like poor performance. Adjusting for case type improved the comparison,
although categories themselves required care: a label such as 'complex' could become another way to influence results.
Fair evaluation therefore needed both consistent definitions and occasional examination of actual cases. The relevant
question was not merely whether two figures had been calculated in the same way, but whether the underlying work was
sufficiently comparable for the comparison to be meaningful.
6. The organisation introduced regular reviews of a small selection of completed conversations. Reviewers examined
whether staff understood the request, explained the outcome and avoided unnecessary exchanges. This took longer than
reading a dashboard, but it revealed patterns that the dashboard could not show. The sample was selected systematically
rather than consisting only of memorable complaints or exemplary successes. Its purpose was not to inspect every
interaction. It was to test whether the numerical trends corresponded to the quality of work managers thought they
represented. Where they did not, the discrepancy became a reason to investigate rather than an embarrassment to be
hidden.
7. The team continued to monitor speed, but stopped treating the shortest response time as an achievement in isolation.
Staff could explain exceptions, and managers reviewed whether the target was producing the intended behaviour. This
approach did not make measurement unnecessary or remove accountability. It made the relationship between the
measure and the purpose explicit. A useful indicator earns its place by helping people understand and improve a service; it
should not be protected merely because it is easy to collect or has appeared in reports for years. When the indicator
begins to distort the work, revising it is part of responsible management.

It is that an unsatisfactory result gives me a next step instead of confirming a permanent judgement about myself.

recordings.MOCK03-LIST-R18: Man: Our team trialled a four-day schedule. I expected the shorter week to make us rush, but we cut unnecessary meetings instead. Woman: That sounds promising. The summary sometimes retained the difficulty but omitted the failed attempt. Staff then suggested the very action the customer had already tried. The sentences in the summary were not necessarily false; the missing relationship made the response unhelpful. We now use the tool to locate relevant messages, but staff read the original before deciding what to do. This costs more time than relying on the summary alone. It also avoids exchanges that would consume time later and damage trust. I am not opposed to the technology. I object to judging its value only by how quickly it produces a readable paragraph. We replaced the identical allocation with a system that recorded preferences and constraints. It was not possible to satisfy every request, so we explained how conflicts would be handled and reviewed the pattern over time. The new rota looks less symmetrical, but people understand its reasoning better. I would still be concerned if the same few people repeatedly carried the difficult work. recordings.MOCK04-LIST-R19: The evaluation of our pilot scheme looked straightforward. We compared attendance before and after the change, and the increase was substantial. I was ready to recommend expansion. A colleague then asked who had stopped attending. That question initially seemed beside the point: the total had risen. But the new participants were mainly people who already used several of our services, while some of the people the scheme was intended to reach had disappeared from the records. We had improved one visible result without establishing that we had met the original purpose. The discovery did not make the increase meaningless, nor did it prove that the change caused every departure. It did mean that our recommendation had outrun the evidence. We conducted follow-up interviews and separated different groups in the analysis. The final recommendation was narrower, with conditions attached to expansion. I found that less satisfying than announcing an unqualified success. It was also more responsible. An evaluation should be capable of changing the decision, not merely supplying impressive figures for a decision that has already been made. Otherwise the appearance of rigour can protect an assumption instead of testing it.
recordings.MOCK04-LIST-R20: I used to believe that publishing all the details of a decision was enough to make it transparent. During a public consultation, we placed the full technical report online and invited comments. Few people responded, and those who did often focused on a minor issue that happened to be easy to understand. We had made the information available without making the decision intelligible. For the next consultation, we explained the alternatives, the criteria being used and the points on which evidence was uncertain. The full report remained available. Some colleagues worried that the shorter explanation gave us too much control over what readers noticed. That was a legitimate concern, so we asked an independent reviewer to check whether important trade-offs had been omitted. The revised process did not remove disagreement. It changed its quality: people could challenge the assumptions that actually shaped the choice. I would not claim that a clear summary is neutral simply because it is clear. Selection always matters. But refusing to select anything can also exclude people, by making participation depend on the time and specialist knowledge needed to interpret an entire technical document.

WRITING MASTERBOOK
Targeted guidance, worked examples and original practice. Use after an attempt, then transfer the correction to a new context.
The four parts: purpose before language
Part 1 has five personal replies of one to five words. Give the requested information directly. Part 2 asks for 20-30 words in
connected sentences. Part 3 has three separate posts of 30-40 words each. Part 4 requires an informal email of 40-50
words and a formal email of 120-150 words about the same announcement.
For a full 50-minute practice, try 3 minutes for Part 1, 7 for Part 2, 10 for Part 3 and 30 for Part 4. These are a training
allocation within the official total, not separate compulsory time limits. Planning and checking belong inside those periods.
Before drafting, identify the audience, every requested action, the facts you must preserve and the word range. A
sophisticated sentence cannot compensate for answering a different question. In the course, B2/B2+ refers to the teaching
target; practice marks are not converted into official Aptis levels.
Part 2: answer both halves economically
Prompt: You have joined a walking group. Explain why you joined and when you can usually attend. Weak answer:
"Walking is very interesting and there are many reasons why people enjoy it." This is grammatical but gives neither the
personal reason nor availability.
Stronger model: "I joined to explore nearby routes and meet people who enjoy walking. I am usually free on Sunday
mornings, although I sometimes work at weekends." (25 words.) The answer spends its limited space on the two
requested points.
Do not add a formal greeting to every short response. Use one or two complete sentences, check articles and prepositions,
and remove general statements that could fit any topic.
Part 3: develop one useful idea per post
A reliable pattern is answer + reason + concrete detail. It is a flexible way of developing content, not a sentence template
to memorise. A comparison may need answer + contrast instead; a personal experience may need event + consequence.
Prompt: Should a club publish notes after meetings? Weak: "Yes, it is good and useful. I agree because it is a good idea
for everyone." The repetition creates length without development.
Stronger model: "Publishing brief notes would help members who cannot attend, especially those working irregular shifts.
The notes need not repeat every comment; they should record decisions and next steps so everyone can prepare for the
following meeting." (36 words.)
Each post has its own purpose. Do not spend the first ten words repeating the question or begin every response with the
same phrase. Personal examples are useful when they clarify the point rather than distract from it.
Part 4: plan one situation for two readers
Read the announcement once for facts and once for implications. Make a short plan for each email before writing either.
For a friend, choose a natural reaction and a shared next step. For an organiser, identify the issue, explain a specific effect
and propose a realistic request.
Example announcement: a weekend workshop has moved to Tuesday afternoon. Existing payments may transfer to a later
weekend course. Do not claim the workshop is cancelled or that refunds are guaranteed. Accuracy about the notice is part
of task fulfilment.
Informal model: "Hi Mia, the workshop has moved to Tuesday afternoon, so I cannot attend after all. I am disappointed, but
we can transfer our payments to the next weekend course. Shall we ask which dates are available and choose one
together? Speak soon, Jo." (43 words.)
Formal model: "Dear Workshop Coordinator, I am writing about the move from Saturday to Tuesday afternoon. I
understand that finding a suitable room may be difficult, but the new time prevents me from attending because I work until
five. Other members may face a similar problem. I appreciate the option to transfer our payments to a later weekend
course. Could you let us know which dates are available and whether our places can be reserved before the new course

opens for general booking? It would also help to receive an outline of the programme, so that we can check whether it
covers the same material. I would be grateful for this information by Friday, when I need to arrange my work schedule.
Thank you for your assistance. Yours sincerely, Jo Patel." (129 words.)
The formal model acknowledges a possible constraint without inventing it as a confirmed fact. It explains the impact, uses
the transfer option correctly and asks for information the organiser could provide. Its polite tone comes from a
proportionate request and clear reasoning.
Register: change the relationship, not only the vocabulary
To a friend: "I am annoyed about the short notice. Could we go next month instead?" To an organiser: "The short notice
makes it difficult to rearrange work commitments. Could you confirm whether a later session is available?" Both are direct,
but the second explains an impact relevant to a decision.
Contractions can be natural in an informal email. Formal writing does not require long words or an apology in every
sentence. "Could you clarify the deadline?" is more useful than "I hereby wish to express my profound desire for
clarification."
A greeting and close should fit the relationship. "Hi Alex" and "See you soon" suit a friend. "Dear Coordinator" and "Yours
sincerely" can suit an identified role when no personal name is supplied. Consistency matters more than inserting
ceremonial phrases.
Paraphrase, cohesion and precision
Preserve the strength of a claim. "May reduce attendance" cannot safely become "will prevent everyone from attending".
Preserve conditions too: "free for members" does not mean "free for all visitors". A useful paraphrase changes wording
while keeping scope, certainty and relationships.
Use connectors to show a real link. However introduces contrast; therefore marks a result; for example introduces
supporting detail. Adding them mechanically can imply a relationship the ideas do not have.
Reduce repetition through reference, not a thesaurus at every noun. After naming "the revised timetable", use "this
arrangement" if the reference is clear. Replacing every repeated word with an unusual synonym can make the message
less precise.
Weak: "The room is small. The room is noisy. The room is not suitable." Stronger: "The room is both small and noisy, so it
may be unsuitable for a discussion involving twenty people." The revision connects evidence to a qualified conclusion.
Edit to the word range without losing the task
Cut empty framing first: "I am writing this email because I would like to tell you that" often becomes "I am writing about" or
disappears. Next remove duplicated reasons, unnecessary quotations and unsupported background. Protect the
requested content points.
If an answer is short, develop the reasoning rather than padding it. Explain who is affected, give one example, or show why
the suggested action is feasible. Count each Part 3 response separately and each Part 4 email separately.
Use one consistent counting convention during practice: words separated by spaces, with contractions and hyphenated
forms counted as one. The actual test provides a counter; follow it when taking the exam. Model counts in these materials
follow the stated practice convention.
A three-pass self-edit
Pass 1, task: mark where you answer each request. Check the announcement facts and the reader. Pass 2, meaning:
check the order of ideas, ambiguous pronouns and whether the request is realistic. Pass 3, language: check your two most
frequent errors, then spelling, punctuation and word count.
Common B2 repairs: "discuss about the plan" becomes "discuss the plan"; "suggest to change" becomes "suggest
changing"; "an advice" becomes "some advice"; "despite it is late" becomes "although it is late"; "I would appreciate if"
becomes "I would appreciate it if".
After correction, record only useful patterns in the Error Tracker. Include the original ID, the reason for the correction and a
new personal example. Revisit it after two days and again a week later. A sentence you can repair once is not necessarily

a pattern you can use under time pressure.

VOCABULARY MASTERBOOK
Targeted guidance, worked examples and original practice. Use after an attempt, then transfer the correction to a new context.
Know what the official tasks ask
Grammar & Vocabulary contains 25 vocabulary questions as well as 25 grammar questions. The vocabulary constructs
are definitions, similar meaning, use in sentence context and word combinations. The mock vocabulary sets in this revision
have five prompts and ten options per set. Follow each set's instructions and read all options.
A synonym task asks for the closest meaning, not a word that can replace the target in every possible sentence. A usage
item requires a choice that fits both grammar and meaning. A combination task depends on conventional usage: knowing
the separate words may not be enough.
For each question, identify what is being tested before choosing. If the gap follows a preposition, an -ing form or noun may
be needed. If several options are grammatical, compare their meanings and the exact context. Do not treat every familiar
expression as the answer.
Learn a unit large enough to use
Record "take responsibility for a mistake", not only "responsibility". Record "a sharp increase in prices", not only "sharp".
Include the usual object or preposition and a short sentence that matters to you.
Useful families of combinations: make a recommendation / raise a concern / reach an agreement / meet a requirement /
draw a conclusion / address a problem / provide evidence / fulfil a commitment. They are related in purpose but do not
share one universal verb.
Common repairs: "do progress" -> "make progress"; "strong rain" -> "heavy rain"; "depend of" -> "depend on"; "an
evidence" -> "a piece of evidence" or "some evidence". Store the corrected chunk and the reason, rather than an isolated
list of wrong forms.
Synonym nuance prevents expensive mistakes
Available means accessible or free to be used; suitable means appropriate for a purpose. A room can be available but
unsuitable. Effective describes achieving a result; efficient adds the idea of avoiding unnecessary time or resources. A
method can be effective but inefficient.
A refund returns money already paid. A discount reduces the price. A deposit is part-payment or security, depending on
the arrangement. These words concern money but cannot be selected simply because a sentence mentions payment.
Plausible means reasonably believable, not proven. Tentative means not final. Inconclusive evidence fails to settle the
issue. These distinctions become important in Weeks 6-8, when a speaker or writer may accept part of a claim while
limiting its certainty.
Prepositions and verb patterns
Learn the whole pattern: responsible for; interested in; compatible with; dependent on; an effect on; a reason for; an
advantage over; access to. A translation from another language may suggest a preposition that English does not use.
Some verbs take a direct object: discuss the issue, explain the rule, affect attendance, request information. Others need a
preposition: respond to a request, apply for a place, refer to a notice, object to a proposal.
After a prepositional to, use a noun or -ing form: look forward to hearing; be accustomed to working; object to paying. Do
not confuse this to with the infinitive marker in "hope to hear".
Confusing words and useful word families
Affect is usually a verb meaning influence; effect is usually a noun meaning result. Advice is a noun; advise is a verb. Rise
does not take a direct object, whereas raise does: prices rise, a company raises prices.
Check the grammatical role before choosing a family member: accurate / accuracy / accurately; clear / clarity / clarify;
significant / significance / significantly; reliable / reliability / reliably. Learning the family is useful when it helps you select a
form in context, not as an exercise in collecting every possible derivative.

Avoid a false upgrade. "Use" does not automatically become better as "utilise". "Help" may be more natural than "facilitate"
in a message to a friend. Lexical range means having appropriate choices and controlling their use.
A retrieval cycle that tests transfer
Day 0: attempt an item before consulting the key. Record the complete correction and one sentence about your own life.
Day 2: cover the phrase and retrieve it from its meaning or a new sentence. Day 7: use it in a short timed response. Day
14: mix it with similar expressions and explain the difference.
If you remember the letter but cannot explain the choice, the exercise has become a memory test of the page. Change the
context. For "raise a concern", write a new sentence about a different service, then contrast it with "rise" in another
sentence.
Mark a tracker entry fixed only after two successful uses on separate days. Repeated errors deserve a small targeted set,
not a longer undifferentiated vocabulary list.
Decision speed without careless guessing
In later weeks, take a first decision promptly, flag genuine uncertainty and move on. Return with a reason: a meaning
distinction, grammar requirement or collocation. Changing an answer merely because another option looks more
sophisticated is not a strategy.
For a five-item matching set, solve clear matches first and then reconsider the remaining options. Do not force a remaining
word into a gap if its meaning does not fit. Read the completed sentence once more before finalising the set.
After a mock, separate unknown vocabulary from misreading, poor time allocation and confusing two known words. The
repair differs: learn a new chunk, slow down at a key qualifier, practise a timed decision, or compare meanings in fresh
contexts.

SPEAKING MASTERBOOK
Targeted guidance, worked examples and original practice. Use after an attempt, then transfer the correction to a new context.
A timed performance with four different demands
Part 1: three personal questions, 30 seconds each. Part 2: one photograph and three responses, 45 seconds each. Part 3:
two photographs and three responses, 45 seconds each. Part 4: three linked questions, one minute to prepare and two
minutes to respond. The component lasts about 12 minutes including instructions and transitions.
The course uses photo briefs because actual photographs and audio files are not included. They support language and
timing practice, but they do not reproduce the visual-processing demand of a photograph. A tutor should keep prompts
visible and withhold feedback until the section ends.
Use a timer you can control rather than relying on a chat model to enforce exact seconds. Record audio if possible.
Pronunciation and intelligibility require an audio sample; a written transcript alone supports feedback on content and
language, not a reliable judgement of pronunciation.
Part 1: answer, extend, stop
Give the answer promptly, then add a reason, habit or brief example. For "How do you travel around your area?", name the
main method, explain why it suits you and mention one exception. You do not need to describe your entire transport
history.
A framework: usual choice -> reason -> concrete detail. Another: present habit -> contrast with the past. These are thinking
routes, not scripts. Select the route that fits the question rather than forcing every answer into the same pattern.
If a question asks about a preference, make your preference clear. A general discussion of what other people like may
sound fluent while failing to answer the personal question.
Part 2: observe before interpreting
Start with the main scene: who or what is visible, the action and the setting. Add one or two relevant details. Use cautious
language for an interpretation: "They may be waiting for instructions" or "It looks as though the event is about to begin."
Do not invent identities, relationships or emotions as facts. "A woman is holding a map" is observable. "She is lost and late
for work" may be speculation. You can speculate, but show the difference in your wording.
The next questions move beyond description. For an experience, give a short event and its consequence. For a wider
question, state a view, explain it and illustrate it. Repeating the photograph description wastes the opportunity to develop
the new prompt.
Part 3: compare on a meaningful dimension
Avoid describing Picture A fully and then Picture B with no connection. Choose a dimension: location, interaction, purpose,
independence, access or effort. State one similarity and one significant difference, then explain what that difference may
mean.
Useful flexible language: "Both involve…", "Whereas the first…", "The second seems more…", "One advantage might
be…", "That would depend on…". Use only what the comparison needs.
Example move: "Both people are learning a practical skill, but one has immediate guidance while the other is working
independently. The first may receive quicker feedback, whereas the second can choose their own pace." The comparison
leads to a consequence rather than stopping at visible objects.
A photograph rarely proves which option is faster, cheaper or more successful. A strong answer can make a reasoned
choice while acknowledging what is unknown.
Part 4: use the preparation minute to map the answer
Read all three prompts. Spend roughly 15 seconds identifying their demands, 25 seconds choosing one personal example
and two main ideas, and 20 seconds arranging the order. Write keywords rather than sentences. Keep every prompt
represented in the notes.

A useful two-minute route is experience (about 40 seconds), explanation or reflection (about 35 seconds), wider opinion
with a qualification (about 40 seconds), and a short final link. These are practice guides, not extra official timing rules.
A framework for change: original situation -> trigger -> response -> result -> broader principle. A framework for evaluation:
position -> reason -> example -> limitation -> judgement. Choose the framework after reading the questions.
Do not spend ninety seconds on the personal story and rush the abstract question. A rich story is useful only if it leaves
time to fulfil the rest of the task.
Extend without rambling
Add a reason when the claim is unexplained. Add an example when the reason is abstract. Add a contrast when a
judgement sounds too absolute. Stop adding detail when it no longer answers the question.
Weak extension: "It is useful, very useful, and important for many people." Better extension: "It is useful for people working
shifts because they can choose when to participate. For example, a recorded introduction lets them prepare before
attending a practical session."
If you run out of ideas, return to the question and ask which part remains unanswered. Repeating the opening with different
adjectives rarely improves task fulfilment.
Self-correction, fluency and intelligibility
Correct an error briefly when it changes the meaning or is easy to repair: "last year - sorry, two years ago". Avoid restarting
an entire answer to fix a minor article. Fluency includes continuing coherently after a small mistake.
Use pauses at idea boundaries. Speak at a pace that leaves room for clear word endings and stressed content words. A
fast stream of words is not automatically fluent, and an unfamiliar accent is not automatically unclear.
When reviewing a recording, identify one place where the listener may lose the message. Is the cause an unclear
reference, unfinished sentence, pronunciation, unnecessary detail or long silence? Repair that specific cause and record
again once.
A focused feedback routine
After a full section, assess task fulfilment, organisation, fluency, grammar, vocabulary, intelligibility and timing. These are
pedagogical review categories, not a calculation of an official Aptis score.
Choose three priorities: one content/organisation issue, one language pattern and one delivery issue supported by the
recording. Write the exact exercise ID in the Error Tracker. Re-record a different response using the same improvement so
that you test transfer rather than memorise a polished script.
Compact tutor command: "APTIS [ID] SPEAKING MODE. Use the attached prompts one at a time; no corrections during
the section. I will control the timer. Afterwards give evidence and three priorities. Assess pronunciation only from audio."
